[h1] THE LOST EPISODE [/h1]



Amazingly good short episode set in the [b]Half-Life[/b] universe, with more or less the same dynamics and a few little improvements and overhaulings over the base game.

Transmissions: Element 120 puts you in the role of an unknown fighter, probably during the events of the Seven Hour wars or shortly after that; it is unclear wether you are, or you are not, Dr. Gordon Freeman (and the ending does not really solve the question, even with... (SPOILER),[spoiler] the mysteryous G-Man calling you "Dr. Freeman", just as in the trailer, with the same line)[/spoiler]. There is a resistance against the Combine, but you do not really get to have them fighting by your side. You are alone, pretty much as the majority of the HL games in which you feel an overwhelming solitude (except when Alyx Vance goes with you, or the army of citizens of City 17).

During your adventure, you get to find a strange device in the shape of a Gravity Gun, but this one casts a strange energy sphere wich explodes with contact on any surface; also, you discover something about the zombies (which you have to discover during the game as it's part of the challenge), and probably one of the most interesting things not only in the game, but the whole HL universe and many other games, is the inclusion of the QRC (Quick Response Codes), which have been sprayed on different walls as hints or help for the hero. By whom? I take, the resistance, but this is also unclear. [spoiler]You eventually find the plaques with the patterns abandoned in some hall, but as every member of the resistante you find is dead, I guess there is no certain way to know this for sure. [/spoiler] There are not too many weapons, but you don't really miss them. And actually the game is so short, you don't really get to use them that much.

Physics are flawless as you could expect from a HL game. And something cool, for serious players, is that the developer doesn't fill you with hints or tutorials or marks or signs telling you what to do. It is you against the enviroment; the player versus the world. Use it; find your way, explore, don't be afraid of squeezing into a tight sewer pipe. Yeah, you'll probably die, or not, but that's how you find the way out (or in).

There are Combine and Zombine (as Alyx named them), and those terrible Stryders. The end comes too fast and unexpectedly, but that doesn't make the game bad, or even feel rushed; it only leaves you with a bitter cliffhanger and, at least in my case, waiting for a sequel or more future content with this little jewel.

This game is basically a perfectly well balanced addition to the universe, and it could hade easily been another episode just like The Lost Coast, which was so well paced and mooded to fit into the saga (with all the mystery and melancholy need to be part of it). 

In short, [b]STOP READING AND GET IT RIGHT NOW.[/b]
